pm_translator.hook: There's ONE job that makes an AI PM different from the ML engineer next to them. It isn't writing models. What is it?
pm_translator.recall: In one line, what is the AI PM's unique value?
pm_translator.answer: translating between business value, user need, and what is technically and data-wise possible

five_shifts.hook: Five things change the moment a product LEARNS from data instead of following rules you wrote. Most PMs can't name two.
five_shifts.recall: Name two ways an AI product differs from deterministic software.
five_shifts.answer: it's probabilistic (right most of the time, not always); data is the raw material, moat AND risk; the metric defines the behaviour; feasibility is uncertain until you build; the human loop (eval, drift, fairness) never fully closes

ai_ml_dl_ds.hook: AI, ML, deep learning, data science - stakeholders smash these together. A PM who can separate them in four sentences instantly sounds credible.
ai_ml_dl_ds.recall: Explain AI vs ML vs DL vs Data Science, one line each.
ai_ml_dl_ds.answer: AI = the goal (machines doing things that need intelligence); ML = achieving AI by learning patterns from data; Deep Learning = ML with multi-layer neural nets that learn features automatically; Data Science = extracting insight from data (overlapping discipline)

paradigms.hook: Every ML system is one of a few learning paradigms. Get the paradigm wrong and the whole data plan is wrong.
paradigms.recall: Give one product example each for supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.
paradigms.answer: supervised = spam filter / churn prediction; unsupervised = customer segmentation; reinforcement = the drone policy or a tutoring policy that optimizes a reward

representations.hook: Vision, speech and language suddenly 'worked' in the last decade. One idea is behind all three.
representations.recall: What is the big innovation that made modern AI work?
representations.answer: learning representations (features) from raw data instead of hand-crafting them - powered by cheap compute, abundant data, and better algorithms

is_it_ml.hook: Before any AI project, the cheapest win is asking whether it's even an ML problem - or just rules in disguise.
is_it_ml.recall: Name two questions from the 'is this even AI/ML?' checklist.
is_it_ml.answer: is there a pattern in data a human could in principle learn? do we have enough representative data? is being wrong sometimes acceptable? would a simple heuristic get 80% of the value?

problem_to_model.hook: Start from the model and you'll force-fit it. Start from the PROBLEM SHAPE and the model family picks itself.
problem_to_model.recall: Match the problem to the model family: predict a number / order a list / produce text / group with no labels.
problem_to_model.answer: number = regression; order a list = ranking/recommendation; produce text = generative; group with no labels = clustering; choose actions for long-term reward = RL

design_for_wrong.hook: Your model WILL be wrong sometimes. The product is defined by what happens in those moments, not the happy path.
design_for_wrong.recall: Name three ways to design for a wrong or low-confidence output.
design_for_wrong.answer: let the user correct/undo, surface confidence instead of presenting a guess as fact, fall back to a default or escalate to a human, and capture the correction as future training data

cold_start.hook: On day one your model is weak - no data yet. If you don't plan for it, the first experience is the worst one.
cold_start.recall: Why is cold-start a product problem, and what do you plan for it?
cold_start.answer: the model has no data so it's weak; plan the first-run experience with heuristics, defaults, or borrowed data until the model is good enough

value_feasibility.hook: You have ten AI ideas and one quarter. There's a simple 2x2 that tells you which to build and which to merely explore.
value_feasibility.recall: How do you prioritize candidate AI initiatives?
value_feasibility.answer: plot business value x technical/data feasibility; do high-value/high-feasibility first; time-box high-value/low-feasibility as research spikes, not committed roadmap

baseline_first.hook: Most ML projects should never have been ML projects. One question kills the bad ones early.
baseline_first.recall: Why must you define a non-ML baseline first?
baseline_first.answer: if a rule or heuristic (even 'predict the average') already hits the bar, the ML project must beat it by enough to justify its ongoing cost - otherwise don't build it

data_is_constraint.hook: Teams obsess over the algorithm. That's almost never what kills an AI product.
data_is_constraint.recall: Why is 'we have a great algorithm' rarely the bottleneck?
data_is_constraint.answer: most AI products fail on DATA - missing, dirty, biased, or not legally usable - not on algorithms; the data strategy is the product strategy

data_leakage.hook: A metrics report can lie to you with a straight face. This is the most common way.
data_leakage.recall: What is data leakage, and how does it fool a PM reading a metrics report?
data_leakage.answer: test data leaking into training inflates the metrics, which then collapse in production; trust only the held-out test/validation score, never the training number

data_readiness.hook: Before greenlighting, run the data through a readiness gate - the same way you'd check legal before launch.
data_readiness.recall: Name two items from the data-readiness checklist.
data_readiness.answer: is it representative of real production inputs? labeled well enough + who labels going forward? do we have rights/consent? does it stay fresh via a pipeline? what biases/gaps exist? what's the non-ML baseline?

mlops_lifecycle.hook: Most PMs think shipping the model is the finish line. It's the start of the expensive part.
mlops_lifecycle.recall: What happens AFTER you deploy a model?
mlops_lifecycle.answer: monitoring and retraining - the long tail; the lifecycle is data -> train -> eval -> deploy -> monitor -> retrain, and the product never really 'ends'

drift.hook: A model that was 95% accurate quietly rots over months. There are two distinct reasons.
drift.recall: Define data drift vs concept drift, with an example.
drift.answer: data drift = the inputs change (new slang, new user mix); concept drift = the input-to-output relationship changes (fraud patterns evolve); both decay accuracy, so you fund monitoring + a retrain trigger

inference_cost.hook: Training is a one-time bill. With LLM products, the scary number is the one that grows with every user.
inference_cost.recall: What is the recurring inference-cost tradeoff for an LLM product, and one way to manage it?
inference_cost.answer: bigger model = better quality but higher latency and per-request cost that scales with usage; manage with smaller models, caching, RAG, or routing easy cases to a cheap model

fairness.hook: A model can be 95% accurate overall and still be a discrimination lawsuit. The aggregate number hides it.
fairness.recall: Why can high aggregate accuracy still be unfair, and how do you catch it?
fairness.answer: it can be 60% for a minority subgroup while 97% overall; measure performance PER subgroup, not just in aggregate

responsible_gate.hook: Before any AI feature ships, there's a gate that separates responsible products from headlines. Six checks.
responsible_gate.recall: Name three items from the responsible-AI ship gate.
responsible_gate.answer: per-subgroup accuracy, explainability to the level the domain needs, privacy (minimal data + consent + deletion), drift monitoring + retrain, a human-in-the-loop/escalation path, and a named owner with a rollback plan

gen_vs_disc.hook: Generative AI is everywhere, but the one-line distinction from 'normal' ML is what tells you when to use it.
gen_vs_disc.recall: Generative vs discriminative - one line each.
gen_vs_disc.answer: discriminative predicts a label (classify/score); generative produces new content (text, image, audio, code) by modeling the data distribution

hallucination.hook: LLMs are fluent and confident - and sometimes confidently, completely wrong. That's a PRODUCT risk, not a bug to wait out.
hallucination.recall: Explain hallucination to a stakeholder, plus two product mitigations.
hallucination.answer: the model produces fluent, confident, false output; mitigate by grounding in your data (RAG), asking for citations, constraining the output format, adding a verification/critic pass, or a human check

rag_ladder.hook: Everyone wants to 'train our own model.' There's a ladder, and you climb only as far as value requires - usually not far.
rag_ladder.recall: Walk the prompt -> RAG -> fine-tune -> train ladder; when do you climb each rung?
rag_ladder.answer: prompt-only first; RAG to ground the model in your own data; fine-tune for consistent style/format or a narrow task; train-your-own only rarely when data is the moat - cheapest rung that works wins

prompt_skeleton.hook: A production prompt isn't a sentence - it has parts, like a function signature. Miss a part and outputs get flaky.
prompt_skeleton.recall: Write a 6-part prompt skeleton from memory.
prompt_skeleton.answer: role/persona + clear task + context/data + constraints + output format + examples (few-shot); add an explicit reasoning instruction (chain-of-thought) for hard tasks

genai_fit.hook: Not every feature should be generative. A short checklist saves you from shipping a hallucinating calculator.
genai_fit.recall: Name two items from 'should this feature use generative AI?'
genai_fit.answer: is the task generative/transformative (not one exact right answer)? can we tolerate or detect hallucination, or do we need RAG + human check? does the input fit the context window and what's the per-call cost/latency? what's the cheapest rung (prompt/RAG/fine-tune)? how do we eval the outputs?

regression_vs_class.hook: Linear regression is the simplest end-to-end model - which makes it the cleanest way to learn the ideas behind EVERY model.
regression_vs_class.recall: Regression vs classification, with an example of each.
regression_vs_class.answer: regression predicts a continuous number (price, demand, time-to-complete); classification predicts a category (spam/not, pass/fail)

least_squares.hook: When we say a model 'learns,' for a line it means something exact and intuitive.
least_squares.recall: What does least-squares actually minimize, in plain words?
least_squares.answer: the sum of squared residuals (residual = actual - predicted) - it finds the line closest to all the points on average

overfitting.hook: A model can score 99% in training and fail in the real world. The gap between two numbers is the tell.
overfitting.recall: Define overfitting via the train/test gap, and how a PM spots it.
overfitting.answer: overfitting = the model memorized the training data and fails on new inputs; a great train score but poor test score (a big train-vs-test gap) is the signal - trust the held-out number

eval_metrics.hook: When a data scientist quotes R-squared or RMSE, a PM should know which one to ask for - and what 'good' means for the decision.
eval_metrics.recall: R-squared vs RMSE - what does each tell you?
eval_metrics.answer: R-squared = fraction of variance explained (0-1, higher better); RMSE = average error in real units, penalizing big misses; ask whether the error is small enough for the business decision it feeds

reading_eval.hook: You'll read more eval reports than you'll write models. Five checks catch the misleading ones.
reading_eval.recall: Name two checks when reading any model's eval report.
reading_eval.answer: is it on a held-out test set (not training)? is the error small enough in real units? any train/test gap (overfit)? does it beat the baseline? does it hold per important segment, not just overall?

aipm_onepager.hook: The capstone is a single page that scopes ANY AI product end to end. Learn it once and reuse it forever.
aipm_onepager.recall: Name the 8 sections of the AIPM one-pager.
aipm_onepager.answer: problem & user (cost of being wrong) -> is AI the right tool? -> data plan -> approach (baseline then model/GenAI rung) -> success metrics (business + model + guardrail, A/B) -> responsible-AI gate -> ops (monitor/drift/retrain/rollback) -> risks & cold-start

metric_defines.hook: Of every decision in an AI product, one is the most dangerous - and the easiest to get casually wrong.
metric_defines.recall: Why is choosing the metric the most dangerous AIPM decision?
metric_defines.answer: the model optimizes EXACTLY what you measure - a wrong or gameable metric produces a confidently wrong product; this is the central AIPM failure mode, so design the metric (and a guardrail metric) deliberately
